=== FILE: #shorts - brains float [1oaiz4Xxuok].en.txt ===

did you know that your brain floats it's very very soft and it's buoyant it floats in a fluid that's made inside the brain the fluid flows through spaces inside the brain and leaks out so the brain is is floating and the reason for this is underneath the brain that's where all the arteries go in and the nerves come out if the brain wasn't floating it would squash the blood vessels it would squash the nerves but if the brain is floating in fluid and the brain is inside a bony box which cannot stretch this means that that soft brain has a certain pressure around it inside the skull and we're trying to send blood to the brain constantly to stay alive that means that pressure has to be higher than the pressure inside the cranial cavity which is great until something goes wrong anatomy and physiology are intrinsically linked you must understand one to understand the other

=== FILE: #shorts - vestibulo-ocular reflex [KP7Yq3A5qA8].en.txt ===

hi my name's sam webster and i teach anatomy at swansea university and here is an ear or euro as we say in wales you may recognize some of the components of the inner ear this is the vestibular apparatus these are the semicircular canals and they detect the rotation of our head and the movement of our head in space but did you know that these are wired to the eye which is why i can do this the link between this and the muscles of your eyes is called the vestibulo ocular reflex and if you want to see what happens when that goes wrong make yourself dizzy and then video your eyes and watch it afterwards if you find this sort of thing interesting too go to the swansea university website and do a search for our audiology courses

Go on. See you later. Hey, look at me. It is 4 weeks after tearing my hamstrings to the day and I'm running again kind of. Now the hamstrings are the muscles in the posterior thigh. They're very big muscles cuz the muscles down there lift your whole body weight and the hamstrings run from the pelvis to the tibia and the fibula. So they cross two joints, which means that they can extend the hip, pushing your foot out behind you, and they can uh flex the knee, so folding the knee joint. When you're running, pushing my foot out behind me isn't too bad. But the other job the hamstrings do is when you bring your leg through forwards, you fold the knee, you flex the knee, and the hamstrings control the extension of the knee before you plant your foot. That's where the muscle gets long and my muscle isn't very long. So, I talked about what happened four weeks ago, but I either tore one hamstring in two places or two hamstrings each in one place. === FILE: 8 cervical spinal nerve roots but only 7 cervical vertebrae #anatomy [APVxTD2yuwg].en.txt ===

Okay, here's a confusing one. In the neck, we have seven cervical vertebrae. C1 2 3 4 5 6 7. But we have eight cervical spinal nerve roots. C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7, C8. So that means in the neck that the C1 spinal nerve root is superior to the C1 vertebrae. And that continues all the way down until we get to the C7 vertebrae. and we have the C8 spinal nerve inferior to it. Now, the reason that's weird is because for the rest of the vertebral column, the numbering is the other way around. So, here's C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7. Here's T1. We know it's T1 because we can see the rib coming from it. Now, all the way down, we'll have the T1 vertebrae, T1 nerve inferior to it. T2 vertebrae, T2 nerve inferior to it. That goes all the way down. Same for the five lumbar vertebrae and the five sacral

=== FILE: A blow to the back of the head #anatomy [Jh6iAqWZyvc].en.txt ===

why is a blow to the back of the head so dangerous uh the bone here is nice and thick the brain is quite well protected well if we turn around to the other side so I've taken the cerebral hemisphere out we can see the durometer here the durometer is the tough connective tissue that's supporting the brain if I take out the brain stem you can see that there's a hole there in the durometer and that's how the brain stem runs from the cerebral hemisphere down to the spinal cord and look at this Leading Edge here of the tentorium cerebell if there's a blow to the back of the head because the brain is floating in cerebra spinal fluid the skull is driven forward and the duramat for with it and that Leading Edge of the tentorium cerebelli is driven into the brain stem now given that the brain stem is where we have our basic functions of driving Consciousness and breathing and heart rate and blood pressure if the brain stem gets damaged that's what kills you

of these sounds not just in terms of sounds but also in terms of language I mean you can even hear a whisper being so sensitive there are mechanisms in the ear that can help protect this apparatus === FILE: Acute pancreatitis can be caused by gallstones #anatomy [sUcEeb__PNs].en.txt ===

Here is the geodinum and the pancreas and the liver. And we can see the bile duct coming in here which is carrying bile from the liver to put it into the geodinum. And we can see the main pancreatic duct here opening into the geodinum. This is carrying enzymes from the pancreas to digest stuff you've eaten. Where the two uh tubes meet, it widens and becomes the ampula of vata. And there is a sphincta, a muscle that closes off this hole, stops stuff going in here called the sphincter ravodi. Now if a gall stone passes down here and gets stuck here where these two ducts meet, not only will it block the bile duct, but it'll also block the main pancreatic duct. This will stop enzymes leaving the pancreas and going into the small bowel. These enzymes are intended to digest stuff you're eating. If they collect in here and get activated, they will digest the pancreas and cause acute pancreatitis. This can be life-threatening because it can move out of the pancreas into surrounding tissues.

=== FILE: Anatomy of butterflies in your stomach [9rS-DiRHpE8].en.txt ===

do you get butterflies in your stomach the gastrointestinal tract is a muscular tube and the parasympathetic nervous system is responsible for secreting making glands secrete into that tube and making those muscles contract in an organized manner to push the contents along rest and digest whereas the sympathetic nervous system um is part of the fight or flight response and when you're nervous or fearful the adrenal glands will secrete adrenaline into the blood and the adrenaline will trigger the sympathetic nervous system to reduce blood flow to the gut to increase blood flow to the heart and to the brain and to the muscles of the limbs so that you can survive but that sensation of reduced blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract is what gives you that feeling of butterflies in your stomach

=== FILE: Arteries and veins #anatomy [Nh7as7c_x5U].en.txt ===

when we look at an anatomy model or an anatomy illustration we typically see that the arteries are painted red and the veins are painted blue uh indicating that arteries carry well oxygenated blood and veins carry poorly oxygenated blood but we have to remember that an artery is a blood vessel carrying blood from the heart to an organ and a vein is a blood vessel carrying blood from an organ back to the heart that's the definition and we particularly need to pay attention at the lungs so this is the pulmonary trunk which is going to give off the pulmonary arteries to the lungs but it's painted blue because it's carrying poorly oxygenated blood from the body to the lungs in the lungs that blood will become well oxygenated so the red vessels here are the pulmonary veins and they're carrying well oxygenated blood back to the left atrium which will go out through the left ventricle and then around the rest of the body so an artery carries blood from the heart a vein carries blood to the heart irrespective of the quality of the blood

=== FILE: Brainstem #anatomy [yNN94OQgy5s].en.txt ===

the brain. And here is the brain stem. The brain stem is the bit that connects the spinal cord with the higher centers like the cerebrum. It has three parts. Down here is the medulla oblongata. This curved bit is the pond and up in there is the midbrain and it's also connected to the cerebellum back here. So much of what goes on in here, we have neurons, we have fibers going up and down. So uh sensory information is coming from the body and going up to the brain and motor information is going out to the the muscles of the body. But also in here we have cells and circuits that use some of that information to manage the basic functions of the body. We have circuits in here that manage blood pressure and heart rate and make you breathe in and out and control your consciousness to keep you awake and regulate movement and drive your gastrointestinal tract. really really basic functions making this a really important part of the body.

=== FILE: Cerebellum learns movement #anatomy [miseS-XLvYE].en.txt ===

The brain has probably got about 86 billion neurons in it and probably 70 billion of them are in here. The cerebellum uh the little brain, these tight folds that we see are giving the cerebellum plenty of surface area for all of those neurons. The reason there are so many neurons here is because the cerebellum is involved in coordinating movement and movement is incredibly complex. In a nutshell, uh sensory and motor innovate information from the cortex passes through the ponds to the cerebellum. Uh complicated circuits in the cerebellum then give information back to the cerebrum to help with movement. So when you intend to make a movement, the cerebellum coordinates that movement. For example, if you're learning to ride a bike, the cerebellum will compare what you intend to do with what actually happens. And as you practice riding the bike, the cerebellum will help make those movements all automatic. So once you've learned to ride a bike, you never forget because all of that movement information is stored in here.

=== FILE: Cornea cells get oxygen directly from the air #anatomy [8HiSY-IswWE].en.txt ===

The sclera and the cornea are the connective tissue parts forming the outer parts of the eye. The sclera is opaque like most connective tissues of the body and it has blood vessels within it. But the cornea is special. The cornea is transparent because it has to let light through it so that we can see. So there are no blood vessels in the cornea. So how do the cells here get oxygen? Um well they get it directly from the air. So tears are pulled across the eye and that protects the cells on the surface of the eye, but it also allows gases to dissolve so that oxygen can pass into the cells and CO2 can leave the cells. There's also a fluid on the deep surface of the cornea and like other tissues of the body that fluid has also got oxygen and nutrients in it which can supply the cells of the cornea. But some of the cornea gets its oxygen directly from the air.

=== FILE: Corticosteroid hormones and the cortex of the adrenal gland #anatomy [F7aMgorx5LY].en.txt ===

Corticosteroid hormones are well they're hormones. Um so they're a very potent signal that's passed into the blood which then passes around the body and acts on cells at a diff distance. They're called steroid hormones because they're made from cholesterol. And they're called corticosteroid hormones because they're made by the cells in the cortex, the outer part of the adrenal glands. Here are the adrenal glands sat on top of the kidneys and up against the diaphragm here. So we're thinking cortisol. That's a corticoststereroid hormone. Cortisol is a hormone that drives metabolism of sugars, fats, and proteins for energy. Also dampens down the actions of the immune system and inflammation. Aldoststerone is also a corticoststeroid hormone that acts on the kidneys to affect sodium retention which in turn affects water and blood volume and then blood pressure. Androgens are made in the cortex which will become testosterone and estrogen. In the middle in the medela we see adrenaline.

=== FILE: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism #anatomy [IRPUYGs-4aU].en.txt ===

uh deep vein thrombosis or a DVT. We're talking about these deep veins here, but also other deep veins in the body. If you're sat still for a long period of time or um led up in bed because you're ill, that can cause the flow of blood through these veins to slow down and that's one of the factors that might cause a blood clot to form inside the vein. This will cause problems locally, but if that clot shifts and moves, it'll flow through larger and larger and larger veins until it gets into the right side of the heart. It will flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle and out through the pulmonary trunk. And then it can go into either of the lungs. And look, in the lungs, the pulmonary arteries are branching and getting smaller and smaller. That means that clot is going to block one of these branches. That's going to cause a pulmonary embolism which will give uh maybe chest pain, maybe a shortness of breath and can be quite dangerous.

=== FILE: Ductus arteriosus in the foetus bypasses the lungs #anatomy [haQ_f8Fw05s].en.txt ===

In the developing fetus, the lungs are not the organs of gaseous exchange and are growing. So there's another mechanism by which blood can avoid going through the lungs and it's this here in the adult after birth. This is the ligamentum arteriosum. But in the fetus, this was the ductus arteriosis. This was a tube, a blood vessel connecting the pulmonary trunk with the aorta. So you've got one oxygenated blood coming from the placenta and the umbilical vein to the right atrium, right ventricle, and then it flows out through the pulmonary trunk. And with the ductus arteriosis, it can flow straight through into the aorta and go off around the body instead of going to the lungs. After birth, when the placenta is disconnected, the prostaglandins being produced by the placenta decrease and the amount of oxygen entering the blood from the lungs now that the baby is breathing increases, causing the smooth muscle in the ductus arteriosis to contract and close.

=== FILE: Foramen ovale in the heart #anatomy [zzR5BiJBs-4].en.txt ===

The right side of the heart sends blood to the lungs. The left side of the heart sends blood around the body. But in the fetus, not a lot of blood can pass through the lungs because they're still growing. So there are adaptations by which blood can pass directly from the right side to the left side of the heart and just go off around the body without going through the lungs. If we look inside the right atrium, we see one of those. It's the fossa ovalis, that depression that we see in the adult. What that did was when blood came in here, it would push through that valve from the right atrium directly into the left atrium and then go off around the body. We can see that here, right atrium, left atrium, there's the fossa ovalis. Uh, with the first breath, huge amount of blood goes to the lungs and comes back from the lungs and the pressure goes up in here and that pushes that flat valve closed, preventing blood from going in that direction. In the embryo that was the forum ovali.

=== FILE: Gastrointestinal tract #anatomy [Hh_P_2yaEhE].en.txt ===

The gastrointestinal tract or the gut is a tube, a muscular tube that runs through the body. The esophagus just carries food to the stomach. The stomach can store the meal and start to digest it and pass little bits of it into the small intestine. The small intestine then is all about surface area and digestion and absorption. It breaks the food down into the smallest molecules. They're absorbed across the cells into the blood. After then the digestion of the nutrients, what's left gets passed into the large intestine. The job of the large intestine is to remove water, remove salts, compact the waste into feces that are stored in the rectum to be removed when convenient.

=== FILE: Great vessels in the chest #anatomy [3P-gGwJLMPA].en.txt ===

Here's the sternum right in the midline. Now, deep to the sternum, we have of course got the heart. But look up here, we've also got what we call the great vessels. These really, really big blood vessels. This is the superior vennea. Inferior vennea is under there. You can see how it's bringing blood from the body into the right side of the heart that then goes out through the pulmonary trunk. It's painted blue because the blood is still poorly oxygenated, but this is an artery. That blood goes to the lungs, gets well oxygenated, comes back from the lungs into the left side of the heart and goes out through the aorta. The aorta really is this big. In fact, it's often even bigger than this. And as it goes around this arch here, it gives off the brachioic trunk, left common corroted artery, left subclavian artery. These are taking blood to the head and neck and the upper limbs. And then the aorta continues around and supplies blood to the whole body. So those are the major vessels we find deep to the sternum.

=== FILE: Grey and white matter of the brain and spinal cord #anatomy [lwD3IXX7yc0].en.txt ===

gray matter and white matter here's a brain here's a spinal cord if we open up the brain we see gray matter around the outside and it's folded to give more room for the gray matter why well in the human brain we maybe have 80 or 90 100 billion neurons in the central nervous system but in the gray matter this is where we find the cell bodies of those neurons and this is where we find the connections and there are possibly a 100 trillion connection c s in the gray matter and that's what gives us our complexity these neurons send information through their axons through the white matter in the middle of the brain and down to the spinal cord where we find the white matter on the outside this is going to and from the brain and the gray matter in the center of the spinal cord connects these neurons to nerves leaving and entering from the body

It's a lot messier. It's a lot muddier. But this is really good fun. === FILE: Heart attacks and atherosclerosis [8rwZ8_bB-vs].en.txt ===

what do we mean by cardiovascular health well blood moves fat around the body to cells that need it fat is an important component of the body if you eat too much fat over decades and decades we start to see fatty plaques forming inside the walls of the arteries this is atherosclerosis immune cells move in and the plaque starts to expand and narrow the artery reducing blood flow to organs that in itself is bad enough but if that plaque breaks a clot will flow off and pass to smaller blood vessels of the body it'll then block an artery if it blocks a coronary artery often the first sign of this is that the heart stops and you die the treatment for this is a good diet and exercise these are the basics of cardiovascular health

=== FILE: Hypothalamus and autonomic #anatomy [ua5OGH-H7gQ].en.txt ===

The hypothalamus is a region in the brain here. It's called the hypothalamus because it's just below the phalamus there. The hypothalamus makes you hungry, drives you to eat food, and then when you've eaten enough food, tells you when to stop. It drives thirst, so you take in water, and again, once you've drunk enough, gets you to stop being thirsty. If you're cold, it tries to make you warm. And if you're warm, it drives blood flow to your skin and makes you sweat to cool you back down again. So it regulates body temperature. It takes light input changing through the day to reset your circadian rhythm and help me balance your sleep wake cycles. It converts action potentials from neurons into hormone production by a direct connection to the pituitary gland releasing things like growth hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone among others. If you've ever wondered where sympathetic and parasympathetic control is in the brain, many of your answers are in here in the hypothalamus.

=== FILE: Inguinal canal very briefly #anatomy [_hD4leEQwRE].en.txt ===

The inguinal canal is a tunnel through the muscles of the abdominal wall. Its function is to allow blood vessels and nerves and the vas deference to run uh between structures in the abdomen and the pelvis and the testice in the male anatomy. Anyway, here we're seeing the vase deference running into the superficial inguinal ring uh the external opening of the inguinal canal. So, it's going to run in that direction. If I take the muscles off there, we see the two ingral canals. So here we're looking at the inside. So there's the deep inguinal ring. Um so we can see the superficial inguinal ring, inguinal canal, deep inguinal ring. And it's made up of the three muscles, external oblique, internal oblique, transverse abdominis, and the transversalis fascia in here. And the floor is formed by the inguinal ligament.

=== FILE: Kidney stones descending in the ureter give a loin to groin pain presentation #anatomy [YMn1APdE3X0].en.txt ===

The ureter is a muscular tube carrying urine from the kidney down to the bladder. Um and in the urine uh stones can form for a number of reasons. And if a stone passes into the ureter, it may block it causing the ureter to become dilated and other spaces in the kidneys become dilated. Um this can give a classical pain presentation that's described as loin to groin. Now, the reason for that is that the muscular tube is trying to squeeze and push the stone along the tube and that can cause colicky pain. And there's not a single nerve that runs with the ureter, rather as the ureter descends, it picks up nerves from different spinal levels. So, as the stone gets pushed along the ureter causing pain, different spinal levels pick up that pain and that pain is referred to different regions of the body. So, as the stone descends, the pain descends in a loin to groin manner.

=== FILE: Mumps and the parotid gland #anatomy [NuIKwtmuEpw].en.txt ===

=== FILE: Muscles of mastication and facial expression #anatomy [iU28Ud027SQ].en.txt ===

In the face we talk about two groups of muscles. We call these the muscles of mastication. Uh these muscles are attached to the mandible and they move the mandible. There are two more in there and they can you know their main job is closing the jaw for biting. They can also protrude the mandible, retract the mandible and move it from side to side for chewing. Whereas these muscles, the muscles of facial expression are attached to the skin. These are the muscles you use to close your eye, close your mouth, to smile, to frown, to make all those facial expressions. The muscles of mastication are innovated by the trigeminal nerve, its mandibular branch. The muscles of facial expression are innovated by a branch of the facial nerve, cranial nerve 7.

=== FILE: Olfactory nerve might grow back after injury #anatomy [Hrif6oySfuQ].en.txt ===

under under the brain under here here is the uh the alactory nerve. This is the nerve that carries smell back to the brain. You can see one on either side and where they run to is here. See these bony depressions? So the alactory bulbs run here to the cribraform plate and then there's lots of little tiny holes in there and they send nerves through those little tiny holes and that takes them to the nasal cavity. Now the interesting thing about the old factory nerve is that if it's injured maybe through trauma maybe a blow to the head tear the tears these nerves off or maybe infection damages these nerves the alactory nerve can grow back. It doesn't always but it can because these little bony tunnels guide the neuronal axons to grow back towards the nasal cavity and they [clears throat] don't have to go very far. So if you're lucky, your smell comes back.

My job is really weird. Um, occasionally people ask me how to get my job. Yeah, we talk about degrees and PhDs and experience in teaching and CVs and universities and stuff like that, but we we never talk about the the weirdest part of it. Um, I guess it's I guess it's kind of a given if you're an anatomy lecturer, you do this part of your job. It's part of your job. You've seen maybe that we teach anatomy using anatomy plastic models. We also use computerenerated models and radioraphs and you know all sorts of uh normal teaching methods. But of course if you're going to teach anatomy, we also use bodies. Bodies that have been incredibly kindly and bravely donated to us to examine after people's deaths. Can you imagine that? donating your body um to a university to be studied by medical students and other health care profession students and anatomy students. I mean, something I'm going to have to do when I die. And really, that's the weirdest part of the job is is about when I die. When you're young, like most university students are, you are invincible. You have your entire life ahead of you. Um, and we know how adolescents and to certain extent young people to a certain extent me uh take part in risky behaviors, right? Because you're invincible, you're pushing your boundaries, you want to feel a lot, you know, all that sort of stuff, right? That that riskreward relationship shift when you're young. But then if you're studying medicine or a health profession course where you're lucky enough to be able to study bodies in anatomy class, um your perception shifts a little bit because this is the first time that the reality of death and your own mortality is put very clearly in front of you every week for a year or two. It it it changes how you think, right? And I've basically got a day of writing ahead of me, which is why I'm making a vlog cuz I'm procrastinating. So, I'm on my way into work. It's a beautiful, sunny, warm Friday morning by the sea. There it is. In South Wales, cuz it's always sunny in South Wales. And oh, the boys are up for the is it the triathlon this Oh no, it's the uh air show this weekend. But don't worry, I'm not going to show you any bodies in this this vlog. Um for the same reason I don't show you any bodies in my anatomy videos. So this This is the the main anatomy lab that you might have seen before if you've watched some of the anatomy videos. This is our lab of plastic models and teaching and computers and all sorts of things. Right? You might have seen we've got lab coats on the wall. So, we've got another lab where we store bodies that we use for anatomical examination for for teaching. And there are a number of clear reasons why we do this and a number of kind of reasons in what we call a hidden curriculum uh for doing this. We've just put 300 students through a physical anatomy spotter exams where we have models and put pins in them and ask them questions and they go around they have a minute at each one. Anyway, so clearly if you want to properly understand the anatomy of the human body, if you have the opportunity to actually study human bodies and look inside them, you get so much more. You see the real sizes, the real shapes, the real arrangement of the bodies. Wow, that nerve is actually that big. You see that while textbooks say that there's a single vein, there's often a couple of vein. You just see well you see reality. All of this stuff is it's simplified and tidied up and made pretty. But when you actually look inside the body, you see the real anatomy. And if you're a health care professional, you can then imagine all of that when you're working with your patient, they've got their skin on or you're looking at their radioraphs. Um, but the other thing is by looking at lots of different bodies, you see another truth, and that is that we are all roughly the same. and we're kind of kind of similar, but if you look at five different people inside, they're all a little bit different. We're all a little bit special. We're all a little bit individual, and we're all a little bit the same. And that's really, really important. Instead of expecting everybody to be laid out like the textbook, you better understand reality. And some aspects of anatomy, you can't see at all unless you look at a real body. I'm thinking about things like fascia. Um, in fact, lots of connected tissue. So, my mind boggles with the number of things you can't see on plastic models, but you can only see on real bodies. But clearly, the strangest thing about all of this is that um we're not just examining a body. We're not just examining examining anatomy. We're examining a person. A person that has died. A person whose time on this earth has ended. And that's incredibly personal. I think I'm thinking about this because it's it's week one. It's week 45 next week. I still got three weeks left of teaching. Then I get a little bit of time off for the summer and then we have our new intake in the first week of September. So I'm always thinking about these new students when they come in, how they're going to feel about all this and how I'm going to prepare them. So that's where my mind is. So this is a very very strange experience. the first time you experience um time with um a body after they've died. And we never forget that. Um I am the designated individual um here at this university, which means I have a legal responsibility for caring for the bodies here. And that's how we think of it. We care for the bodies. Um students will often um be told that this is the first patient, right? We never forget that the body in front of us is the body of a person that has donated their body for us to examine. So we don't treat the body as a number. We don't treat the body as a piece of anatomy. We treat the body as a person. And we're incredibly careful and respectful and uh grateful. And just just imagine how big and important that is to a health care professional to be able to have this experience in a safe environment like the anatomy department rather than having it for the first time in a clinical environment where you are expected to behave in a certain way and handle it. We give students the opportunity to go through those emotional processes and those difficulties um over the two years that they study anatomy with us. So then I I don't know that anatomist ever talk about this with each other but imagine how that affects us. So me as a teacher I've been working with bodies to study anatomy for uh well 32 years which is quite a long time and getting used to it is the wrong you never get used to it you never take it for granted it's always special but you have a constant reminder in front of you every week that this is going to be you one today. So then, if you know what I do for a hobby, being a rock climber and a mountaineer and that sort of thing, you must wonder, blimey, how on earth can you do all the things that you do knowing, I don't know. === FILE: Pleura link the lung to the diaphragm and ribs #anatomy [P6TRVD8bclY].en.txt ===

Each lung is covered by a thin membrane called the plura. It's a cirrus membrane. And then the inside of the thoracic wall and the diaphragm are also covered by plura. And also this side of the heart. Um and in between those two layers of plura, there's a potential space, the plural cavity. Really in there, there's a vacuum with a little bit of fluid. Now when the diaphragm moves and when the ribs move because the parietal plura is stuck to them it moves with the diaphragm and the ribs because there's a vacuum between the parietal plura and the visceral plura. The visceral plura has to move with the parietal plura because the visceral plura is stuck to the lungs. The lungs have to move with the visceral plura. And that is how the movements of the diaphragm and the rib cage are translated to the movements of the lung. That's how we breathe. The plural.

=== FILE: Scaphoid bone fractures #anatomy [FVkrev2w1yk].en.txt ===

The scafoid bone is the most commonly fractured bone of the wrist. These are the wrist bones, the carpal bones here. They they slide over each other a lot better in real life than they do in this skeleton. And see where the scafoid bone is? Look, here's the thumb. Here's the radius. So, this means that well, it means that the scafoid is here. But that means that if you fall onto an outstretched hand, the force goes through the scafoid to the radius, which is why it's so commonly fractured. And we worry about scafoid fractures because the arteries that supply blood to the hand send arteries back through the scafoid, which means that if it's fractured, there's a risk that the proximal part of the bone will lose its blood supply. If that happens, then we'll see necrosis of the bone and in the future we'll see osteoarthritis and pain and wrist dysfunction. So you want to make sure that the scafoid bone heals properly if you suspect that it's fractured.

=== FILE: Superior vena cava and inferior vena cava bring blood of the body back to the heart #anatomy [DMOA1da-d30].en.txt ===

So the aorta is the main artery taking blood away from the heart and taking it around the body. There it is back there. But what are the veins that bring all the blood from the body back to the heart? Well, we have the superior vennea up here and the inferior vennea down there. So the superior vennea is made by the two brachiophalic veins which themselves are made by the internal jugular vein and the subclavian vein. So the superior vennea is getting blood from the head, the neck, the upper limbs and the chest and taking that into the right atrium. Whereas the uh the inferior vennea is actually in the abdomen. So the inferior vennea is taking blood from the lower limbs, the pelvis, the abdomen and look the heart sits on the diaphragm. So as soon as the inferior vennea goes through the diaphragm and into the chest, it's in the heart. So the superior vennea and the inferior vennea bring the blood of the body back to the heart.

=== FILE: Tears move across the eye and into the nose through the nasolacrimal duct #anatomy [7p8bEO9KZf0].en.txt ===

Here is the eye. Uh it's a right eye. So that's lateral. That's medial. This is the nose over here. And this is the lacrimal gland. So the lacrimal glands make tears. Uh we can see the lacrimal gland and its ducts there. So it puts tears onto the surface of the eye onto the cornea and the reta and the sclera. And in doing so, it protects this surface of the eye and nourishes the cells here, stops them from drying out. And when you blink you pull your tears from this corner down to this corner. And in here we can see a couple of little pupa couple of little holes and they allow the tears to pass into these canaliculi which drain them into this hole here. That's the nasol lacrimal duct. Now the nasol lacriml duct takes those tears and puts them in the nasal cavity in there. So that's why you you don't notice your tears moving across the eye all day. And that's why your nose runs uh when you cry.

=== FILE: The Achilles (or calcaneal) tendon #anatomy [MoAIFSvlVMQ].en.txt ===

Here is the Achilles tendon. Um, I think it's the longest, strongest, and thickest tendon in the body. Its modern name is the calccanial tendon because it attaches to the calccanous, this bone here. And calccanous is a general term for the heel. Notice how the calccanous sticks out posteriorly. So, this tendon pulling on this gives a bit of leverage around the pivot point here. And by sticking out posteriorly, we've got bit more of a base to stand upon. Um the purpose of the Achilles tendon is to attach the muscles gastromus sleas and plantaris which is a little diddy muscle on the deep surface to the calccanous. These muscles are very powerful plant flexors that let you stand on your toes. Plantaris I don't think it's on this model and doesn't exist in 10% of people either. This tendon is a little bit special to humans. It it massively increases our efficiency in walking and running and gives you a much higher top speed.

=== FILE: The cornea becomes cloudy after death because endothelial cells stop pumping water out #anatomy [vYaNRzetr5I].en.txt ===

I've got another cornea fact for you. So the cornea, my cornea in this plastic model is starting to go a little bit cloudy. And that's what happens after death. The cornea is transparent because the collagen fibrals are arranged absolutely perfectly to create a connective tissue that's also optically transparent. One of the ways in which this happens is that the deepest layer of cells, the endothelial cells, they have ion pumps that move ions in such a way that water is pulled out of the cornea osmotically to help those collagen fibrals align themselves perfectly within the tissue. After death, there is no energy available to those endothelial cells. So they can't do that function anymore. So water passes into the cornea disrupts that perfect arrangement of collagen fibrals and the cornea becomes cloudy. The rate at which that happens depends upon whether the eye is closed or open after death.

=== FILE: The hyoid bone is a weird bone #anatomy [3c9VrR7vGtc].en.txt ===

The hyoid bone is a weird bone. What are you doing under there? There it is. It's a U-shaped bone. And it's weird because it's not actually articulating with any other bones. What we can see though is we can see there are lots of muscles pulling on the hyoid bone from every direction. So, it's suspended by all of these muscles. The tongue sits on top of it. So, muscles of the tongue attached to it. Here we can see the larynx. So the larynx is hanging from the hyoid bone. And the larynx of course is important for speech and breathing. And the larynx moves up and down when we swallow. So if you move the hyoid bone up and down, the larynx moves up and down. And that sends food down the esophagus and not down the airway. So the hyoid bone is really important. Um, and wouldn't everything look quite different if it didn't exist here? How would all these muscles run? How would we do all of this?

=== FILE: The liver has an artery and a vein bringing it blood #anatomy [jwBWIK425OA].en.txt ===

The liver has two blood vessels bringing it blood um and different blood. Uh in red we see the hippatic artery proper. This is a normal artery carrying normal arterial blood. So nicely oxygenated blood and all that to the liver. And the other one in purple is the hippatic portal vein and it's much larger. It's a vein because it's carrying blood from a tissue back to the heart. It's a portal vein because it's carrying blood from one tissue to another tissue before it goes back to the heart. So the hippatic portal vein is carrying the blood of the gastrointestinal tract. So this is blood which is poorly oxygenated now because it's been used by these tissues but rich in nutrients because the gastrointestinal tract has been absorbing nutrients. All of that blood from both of those vessels then passes across the hpatocytes through the liver. The hpatocytes can do work on that blood and the blood returns to the inferior vennea which the liver wraps around and goes back to the heart.

=== FILE: The name of an artery sometimes changes along its length #anatomy [cxrOcVpVfts].en.txt ===

Here's a weird one. Sometimes we change the name of an artery as it runs through the body. Not because it branches, but because of where it is. For example, here's the subclavian artery here coming off the arch of the aorta. So, it's subclavian artery and then it runs over the first rib. We can see on the other side here, too. So, it's the subclavian artery as far as the first rib. And then when this artery passes the first rib and moves into the armpit, the axilla, we now call it the auxiliary artery. We can see that here as well. There's the auxiliary artery running through the axilla. When that same artery leaves the axilla and enters the arm, we call it the brachial artery because brachial means arm. So this is the brachial artery and then it ends properly here as it divides into different arteries, the radial artery and the ulnar artery that supply blood to the hand. We do this not to make it difficult to learn. We do this to make it easier to communicate accurately.

=== FILE: The thalamus is a sensory filter in the brain #anatomy [ljLd1mRhMyM].en.txt ===

Here is the phalamus under there. And here there's the phalamus. There are two phalamuses on the left and right. So they're they're deep within the brain here, the gray matter. They're collections of neurons. The reason the phalamus is so interesting is because we typically describe these as the sensory saves, the sensory relays, the sensory filters of the body. You are covered in senses and all of your sensory information except for smell goes through the phalamus. Now the circuits in the phalamus determine what's important and what's not. So you don't tend to feel your clothes on your skin all day because the phalamus determines that's not interesting. Filters it out. Doesn't send it on up off up to the cerebrum. But as soon as a fly lands on your skin, the phalamus determines that is important. Sends that signal up to your cerebrum and you are aware of it. There are other functions uh memory and emotion and that makes sense because those things are also involving sensory inputs.

=== FILE: Thymus is not a gland it is part of the immune system #anatomy [i2Mhuf5dhGQ].en.txt ===

The thymus is not a gland. Here it is. The thymus is most active during fetal life and childhood. It's part of the immune system. It's a primary lympoid organ. Um tlymphosytes from bone marrow throughout the body. Those cells move to the thymus and in the thymus they mature. What's happening generally speaking is that tlymphosytes are tested against tissues of the body. If they react to tissues of the body, they're discarded. But if they look like they're going to become useful members of the immune system, they're kept and then they go on and live in the lymphoid tissues, the immune system in the body. Now, two things can go wrong with this. One, if the thymus doesn't form properly, then the immune system won't form properly. So, immuno deficiency, an immune system that's not working. But also on the other hand if those Tlymphosytes that react to tissues in the body are not discarded you can develop autoimmune diseases where your immune system attacks your own tissues.

=== FILE: Thyroid surgery, recurrent laryngeal nerve and a hoarse voice #anatomy [0EYzTlqgEFw].en.txt ===

recurrent Lal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve so after the vagus nerve has descended into the chest the recurrent Lal nerve branches and ascends back up the posterior corner of the trachea now look at this here's the thyroid gland here and here and the thyroid gland wraps around the trachea if the thyroid gland has to be removed surgically often because of thyroid cancer then the recurrent Lal nerve is at risk of injury because it's innovating the muscles that move the vocal cords in the larynx and you need to bring your vocal cords close together to make a strong sound if the nerve is injured the vocal cord on this side becomes paralyzed and that gives a horar voice and difficult to make a strong sound

=== FILE: Why do we have kneecaps？ #anatomy [SfnHKMK9x2o].en.txt ===

why do we have kneecaps well this is the patella uh and the patella is a sesamoid bone which means it's a bone within a tendon and it's within the tendon of the big quadriceps femoris muscle of the thigh quadriceps femoris is job is to extend the knee uh we often find sesamoid bones in tendons that are running over other hard bits of anatomy and what it does is for one it pushes the tendon a little bit further away from the bone giving a mechanical advantage the tendon inserts in here but also of course when you kneel down your patella protects your soft articular cartilage and other structures kneecaps yeah I'm sure they're very handy

=== FILE: Why does my nose get blocked？ #anatomy [_xNS--GVbnw].en.txt ===

why does my nose get blocked well here's the nasal cavity in here and there is a a midline septum separating the left and right sides this is a mucosa imate mucus and in here is an erectile tissue so when blood flows through that erectile tissue it can expand and it'll swell to fill that space in truth one side is always blocked and which side is blocked swapped every 6 hours or so you breathe through one side or the other but if you have an infection bacterial or viral um or maybe hay fever a reaction to pollen can cause inflammation will also cause this to swell and look there isn't actually a lot of space in there the air flows through a narrow space it doesn't have to swell much to block the nose

Did you know that your spinal cord does not run all the way down your vertebral column? It did when you were a fetus, but your bones, your vertebral column grew faster than your spinal cord did. And if you're an adult, your spinal cord ends here at about the L1 L2 vertebral level. Um, this part of the spinal cord here at the end is called the conus medelaris. And what we're seeing here is we're seeing spinal nerves running down the vertebral canal before they leave between vertebrae. And this makes a structure that gets called the horse's tail, the corderina. The other structure in here is the phylm terminalei which runs from the end of the spinal cord all the way down to the coxix and anchors it uh in place there.
